prop: A census check cannot be built on labels, and the record model already shows the right way to extend the schema. At mint time only key, label, world_root and world_state survive into an ExtentEntry — the observation's kind is dropped, and the grep pattern exists only inside a display label, where an author-chosen pattern containing " in " or "(grep: " would make parsing ambiguous. The census therefore needs the new root-level search entry to carry two structured fields into ExtentEntry — the observation kind and the search pattern — following the exact precedent world_root set: #[serde(default)], with the empty value read as "predates the field, not eligible" rather than guessed about. Legacy facts can then never satisfy a census requirement, whose remedy is precisely to re-run the grep under the new capture. The snapshot already ships facts.jsonl with full extent entries, so check reads these fields from files every snapshot already contains; and because no surface lets an author supply an extent by hand, both sides of the rooting comparison and the pattern are tool-captured by construction.

prop: The decidable trigger is declaration (candidate 1): a modification target is a structured record the author creates — a symbol string plus a fact citation — and the refusal fires only on a declared target whose cited fact carries no qualifying census entry. This sits inside the machine partition's own stated principle, that machine failures are "objective contradictions between a document and the record it claims to rest on, decidable without a human": a target row is exactly a pointer at evidence, and "you did not point at your evidence" is the README's own example of a decidable question. The refusal's remedy is singular — run the workspace-rooted grep for that symbol, mint the fact, cite it (or withdraw the target) — so refusal rather than report is the right disposition for the declared-but-uncensused case, by the same discriminator under which scope.rs chose report: there, only a person can tell context from conclusion; here, nothing is left to tell.

prop: Under-declaration — the memo recommends modifying a symbol it never declared — cannot be a refusal and must not be silently absorbed either. Deciding from prose that a sentence "tells an implementer to modify X" is a heuristic read of English, exactly the class the charter routes to the human-owed partition or nowhere; scope.rs's measured precedent shows the symbol-detector that trigger would need flags quotation and misses conclusion. The design therefore makes the omission visible instead of detected: (a) once a workspace declares any target, render emits a Modification targets section, and once any claim exists it emits the section even when empty — "Modification targets: none declared" — so a memo that recommends changes while declaring nothing shows a hole where the census should be, in front of every reader; and (b) check's standing non-coverage list, whose first entry is already "dependents that never declared themselves", gains a census-specific line ("a recommendation whose target was never declared") so the blind spot is printed rather than implicit.

prop: "Transcribed verbatim" cannot be an honour-system field, and does not need to be: the decidable relation is that a premise's text is refused unless it is a verbatim substring of the cited donor fact's captured output. Both sides of that comparison are Strings the tool controls — a fact's output is produced only by look/run (file bytes read verbatim by look_path, grep match lines, a process's merged stream), no authoring surface lets anyone supply output by hand, and output is immutable after mint — so substring containment is a pure byte-level comparison with no normalisation step owned by the check. Typing is the selection mechanism, not the trust: the author types the premise, but a typed premise the donor never wrote fails containment and is refused at the verb. This is exactly the README's Direction item for supporting-span selection ("refused unless it is a verbatim substring of a cited fact — the author cannot type an extent, and here could not invent support, only select it"), and TET-29 is the first place it becomes load-bearing rather than roadmap.

later.note: The README Direction item exists as claimed: "refused unless it is a verbatim substring of a cited fact" and "the author cannot type an extent, and here could not invent support, only select it" are both verbatim; the memo's quote joins them with a dash, eliding the intervening "The dual of the extent guarantee:" — all quoted words are exact and in order, so the identification stands. The item sits under Direction (roadmap), not under What exists today.

Both sides of the containment comparison are tool-controlled Strings: facts.rs deliberately exposes no surface that accepts extent or output text, FactEvent::Revise has no output field so output is immutable after mint, and only look/run write the pending buffer a fact is minted from (observe.rs, F4).

The capture-side premises are all stated by the code: observe.rs's module doc makes look/run the only two ways into the pending buffer; facts.rs's module doc says there is deliberately no flag by which a caller supplies extent or output; FactEvent::Revise carries no output field at all, so output is immutable after mint. A typed premise the donor never wrote therefore has nothing to be contained in, which is the claim's mechanism.

The README Direction bullet is the supporting-span-selection item, and both quoted fragments are verbatim in it; the memo's quotation splices them with an em dash, eliding "The dual of the extent guarantee:" without changing meaning. The same README lists "Requiring a transplanted mechanism to carry its donor's stated premises" under Direction, i.e. roadmap — consistent with "the first place it becomes load-bearing rather than roadmap", and no span-selection verb exists anywhere in src/.

prop: An undischarged premise must be a legal workspace state, so the ticket's refusal cannot all move to the verb the way TET-28's did. The instrument works by transcribe-first: the author selects the donor's premises before knowing whether each holds at the destination — the confrontation the section exists to force. Refusing a premise row that cites no claim at declaration time would demand the destination-holds claim exist before the premise can be recorded, inverting that order (answer first, transcribe after) and pushing an author who cannot yet discharge a premise toward not declaring it at all — the same "refusing would make the honest case unwritable to catch the dishonest one" failure scope.rs's discriminator names. TET-28 never faced this because a census either exists or does not; a premise inventory is built across time. So the workspace invariant enforced at the verb is only "every premise is a genuine quotation of the cited donor's capture" (plus: donor fact exists and carries span boundaries, destination target exists and is live, a discharge cites an existing live claim); "every premise is discharged" is not a workspace invariant at all — it is a property of the finished document.

later.note: The discriminator C8 invokes is scope.rs's, verbatim at lines 49-50: "Refusing would make the honest case unwritable to catch the dishonest one." The transcribe-first argument applies it as written — a declaration-time discharge requirement would invert the order the instrument exists to force, and the conclusion (which invariants are verb-enforced vs document-level) follows from stated, verified premises.

The contrast with TET-28 is accurate: targets.rs moves its whole refusal to the verb precisely because "a census either exists or does not" — declare() refuses at declaration and "render therefore needs no refusal of its own" — whereas a premise inventory built across time has a legal intermediate state, which is the asymmetry C8 asserts.

The named discriminator exists byte-for-byte in scope.rs ("Refusing would make the honest case unwritable to catch the dishonest one."), and the contrast with TET-28 is accurate: targets.rs's census predicate is decidable at declaration because a census either exists in the cited fact's extent or does not, with no state built across time. The argument that discharge-at-declaration would invert transcribe-first is the design's own reasoning, and it applies that discriminator to the case it names rather than misquoting it.

prop: The rendered section follows compose.rs's shipped conventions with one deliberate difference. A "## Transplants" section renders beside the modification-target section: per live transplant, the donor fact id with its extent labels (labels, never absolute keys — the committed-document rule), the destination target id and symbol, and one entry per live premise carrying the selected text verbatim in a fenced block with the discharging claim id beside it; withdrawn transplants and premises are dropped, and once any claim exists the section renders even when empty ("none declared"), because the hole is the finding — the same visibility answer to under-declaration the target section shipped. The deliberate difference: compose.rs refuses to inline captured output into the document because output is unbounded, but a premise is an author-bounded selection, not a whole capture, so inlining it verbatim is both safe and the entire point — the reader must see the donor's clause on the page, spelled the way the donor's file spells it, or the section is a list of opaque pointers. Fenced blocks rather than table cells because a premise legitimately spans lines and markdown table cells cannot carry multi-line verbatim text without escaping, which would violate byte-fidelity.

later.note: Every convention cited is shipped in compose.rs: labels rendered, never absolute keys ("a committed document should not carry /Users/<someone>/..."); the target section renders when empty once any claim exists, doc'd as "Because the hole is the finding"; withdrawn records are dropped; captured output is not inlined because "It is unbounded (a run can capture megabytes)" — so a bounded author-selected premise is genuinely the deliberate difference, not a contradiction; and ledger_cell replaces newlines with spaces because a markdown table row is one physical line, supporting the fenced-block choice for multi-line verbatim text.

The conventions the section claims to follow are compose.rs's shipped ones: render_targets renders once any claim exists, as "None declared..." when empty, because "the hole is the finding"; withdrawn records are dropped; render_facts renders labels and never absolute keys, for exactly the committed-document reason; and captured output is deliberately not inlined because "It is unbounded (a `run` can capture megabytes)" — so the claimed difference (an author-bounded premise selection is safe to inline) is a genuine, correctly characterised departure rather than a contradiction. The fenced-block rationale is also grounded: ledger_cell must replace embedded newlines because a markdown table row is one physical line, which would break byte-fidelity for multi-line premises.

prop: This design recommends 32768 bytes (32 KiB) as the bound, declared in the source as a judgement and not as a measurement. Its only stated constraint is that it be strictly below whatever cap the caller applies, and since tetel cannot observe that cap the value is chosen conservatively; its consequence on the nine censuses measured here is that seven of them (claim, fact, check, prose, ack, render, get) return bounded and two (target at 24974 bytes, label at 8201) return whole.

later.note: The consequence is reproduced with margin. Rebuilding look_grep's exact grep invocation, the seven censuses claim/fact/check/prose/ack/render/get come to 162183/124840/123826/81081/74680/61431/44497 bytes of stdout alone, every one far above 32768; target and label come to 24261 and 7488 bytes of stdout, and to 24975 and 8202 as full returns (stdout plus the `({note})\n` exclusion line, whose byte-exact reconstruction is 714 with the six-memo list that predates this memo's own .md). The stated 24974 and 8201 are exactly those returns less the trailing newline, so both figures are reproducible under a stated convention. Worth knowing, not a defect: these two numbers embed the exclusion note, which lists rendered memo paths, so they drift as memos are added — the seven-bounded/two-whole conclusion does not.

prop: The acknowledgement event cannot live in `prose.jsonl`. `ProseEvent` is an internally-tagged serde enum over exactly `Create` and `Revise`, and `workspace::read_jsonl` propagates any line's parse failure as an error over the whole log rather than skipping it; empirically, a build at this pin reading a `prose.jsonl` containing one valid `Create` line and one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line fails the entire read with `unknown variant \`Ack\`, expected \`Create\` or \`Revise\`` and exits 1. A new tag value therefore makes every older build unable to read even the prose it already understood.
note: binding: Evidence shows an acknowledgement event present in prose.jsonl, contradicting the claim that it cannot live there.

later.note: ProseEvent is `#[serde(tag = "event")]` over exactly Create and Revise; read_jsonl `?`-propagates any line's parse failure over the whole log; and the binary built from this worktree, reading a prose.jsonl with one valid Create line plus one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line, exits 1 with `unknown variant `Ack`, expected `Create` or `Revise``.

Reproduced at this pin: a probe workspace whose prose.jsonl holds one valid Create line and one `{"event":"Ack",...}` line makes `tetel query prose` exit 1 with `unknown variant `Ack`, expected `Create` or `Revise``, returning none of the valid line. Backed by F3 (ProseEvent is `#[serde(tag = "event")]` over exactly Create and Revise) and F5 (read_jsonl propagates the per-line parse error with `?` over the whole read).

prop: The acknowledgement log is re-homeable into TET-36's obligation ledger without rewriting a single event, because no field in it is specific to this residue. It records a block id, the block's text and citation list, a digest per cited claim, a reason and a timestamp; it records none of the quantities `prose_after_proof` derives — not the anchor, not any claim's first proof, not the block timestamp, not whether the block was listed. A general ledger consuming these as discharge records for one obligation class therefore needs the events as they stand and a rule that reads them, which is a re-homing rather than a rework.

later.note: The quantities prose_after_proof derives are exactly the anchor, each claim's first-proof timestamp, the block's first-appearance timestamp and the listed/not-listed decision (checks.rs:414-557), and none of them appears in the event schema C8 specifies — that schema is block id, text, cite list, per-claim digest, reason, timestamp, all of which are inputs or authorial content. The re-homing conclusion is a statement about TET-36's unwritten ledger and was not independently checked, but nothing in the schema contradicts it.

The quantities `prose_after_proof` derives are the per-claim first proof, the per-block anchor (`cited.iter().map(...).max()`), the block timestamp, and the listed/not-listed decision — none of which appears among the five fields C8 defines plus the timestamp. Every field the ack records (block id, text, cite list, digest per cited claim, reason, time) is a generic discharge record, so re-homing it needs a new consuming rule rather than an event rewrite.
